profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting at a mid-sized B2B SaaS company preparing a pilot of a SPRINT-style estimation workflow for the next release planning cycle. The company wants to use quantitative delivery curves from prior work, grouped into clusters of similar projects, to forecast effort and defect discovery for an upcoming platform initiative that spans billing, permissions, and reporting services. The meeting is between the engineering manager sponsoring the pilot for quarterly planning and the staff data engineer who would assemble the historical data, context descriptors, and clustering workflow. Their agenda is to decide what historical project data will feed the pilot, what context fields will characterize clusters, which internal dataset will be treated as the baseline, who owns each setup step, and what exactly should exist by next Friday's planning checkpoint. The expected outcome is an apparently shared pilot plan: assemble historical project data, attach context fields, generate an initial forecast for the new initiative, and have the pilot ready for planning next Friday.

members.name: Nina Patel
members.expertise: Release planning, roadmap forecasting, cross-team execution
members.background: Nina manages three product engineering squads and regularly prepares material for quarterly planning reviews using Jira rollups, release burndowns, and post-launch summaries. She is interested in bringing more empirical structure into estimation, but her interaction with engineering data is mostly through management-facing reports rather than raw operational systems.
members.private_state: Nina wants a lightweight pilot that can influence the upcoming planning discussion without asking squad leads to learn a new process or defend technical analytics details in front of directors. She is trying to produce something credible and easy to consume quickly, even if some parts are manually assembled behind the scenes.
hidden_assumptions: When someone says 'historical project data,' it naturally means completed, planning-visible feature epics from the last few release cycles because those are the only comparisons leadership will recognize as legitimate precedent.

A pilot being 'ready for planning next Friday' means she has a concise planning artifact she can bring into the meeting: a forecast summary, a few similar-project examples, and labels that make intuitive business sense.

Useful 'context fields' are the descriptors that explain why one project is comparable to another in planning conversations, such as team size, customer commitment level, legacy-system touch, and whether work crossed product boundaries.
If they use 'the standard dataset,' it should match the release analytics view already used in leadership reviews, since consistency with familiar numbers is part of credibility.

members.name: Leo Martinez
members.expertise: Engineering analytics, time-series normalization, internal data tooling
members.background: Leo maintains the engineering metrics warehouse and has built internal pipelines for cycle time, incident correlation, and service-level delivery trends. He has experimented with clustering delivery curves before and sees the SPRINT-style pilot as a chance to create a reusable estimation foundation rather than another one-off planning spreadsheet.
members.private_state: Leo wants the pilot to be methodologically clean enough that, if it works, it can be reused each quarter without manual cleanup. He is wary of producing a hand-tuned management summary from loosely filtered projects because that would make the approach look arbitrary and harder to operationalize later.
hidden_assumptions: When someone says 'historical project data,' they mean the full candidate population in the warehouse that can be normalized into comparable curves, not just the subset that happened to appear in planning decks.

A pilot being 'ready for planning next Friday' means the ingestion, normalization, clustering, and context-tagging flow is reproducible end to end, with a forecast run that can be regenerated rather than manually curated.

Useful 'context fields' are the stable explanatory variables already available or codable from systems of record, such as repository spread, dependency fan-out, service ownership count, and interrupt load.
If they use 'the standard dataset,' it should be the engineering warehouse snapshot used for analytical work, because that is the authoritative source before management-layer aggregation and cleanup.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to build the pilot from 'historical project data.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nina means completed feature epics from the last four release cycles that were visible in planning and have stable, presentation-friendly records.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leo means the broader warehouse population of delivery efforts over roughly two years, including work packages and some still-open initiatives if their curves can be normalized and compared.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds like a technical planning term rather than an active decision, so each person assumes the inclusion boundary is obvious: Nina from a planning-precedent lens, Leo from a data-population lens. Because both think they are merely referring to the sensible historical base, the gap stays implicit.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'add context fields' to characterize clusters.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nina means manager-readable labels such as team size, customer visibility, legacy touch, cross-team coordination, and launch commitment pressure.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leo means mostly machine-usable technical descriptors such as repo count, service count, dependency degree, incident load, and ownership dispersion, with business labels added later only if needed.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both strongly endorse the need for context and use the same phrase naturally, but each treats their own class of context as the obvious default. Since neither is rejecting context itself, the disagreement hides inside what kind of context feels self-evidently useful.

misalignment_points.topic: What 'ready for planning next Friday' means as a deliverable
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the pilot should be 'ready for planning next Friday.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nina means she should have a usable planning artifact by then: a manually polished summary of the forecast, two or three similar-project clusters, and enough explanatory labels to support the roadmap conversation.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leo means the pilot is only truly ready if the core workflow is reproducible end to end, so the forecast and cluster assignments come from a working pipeline rather than a one-off manually assembled view.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are deadline-oriented and sincerely believe they are defining the same milestone. 'Ready' sounds complete enough on the surface, but each silently applies a different success standard: presentation-ready usefulness versus reproducible-system completeness.

misalignment_points.topic: Which dataset is the standard baseline
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to use 'the standard dataset' so the pilot lines up with existing reporting.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nina is thinking of the release analytics export used in leadership reviews, where work is grouped by release and cleaned up after retrospectives.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leo is thinking of the engineering metrics warehouse snapshot used for internal analysis, where work is grouped by detected project start and refreshed routinely for modeling.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both sources are commonly referred to inside the company as the standard engineering data because they originate from the same systems and produce familiar trend charts. The phrase feels precise enough in conversation, so neither realizes they are pointing at different concrete artifacts.
